title: Who would raise your children? A guardian checklist
dek: Choose a willing guardian and backup, separate immediate care from court appointment, and record the ordinary details a caregiver would need.
metaDescription: Choose a willing guardian and backup, separate immediate care from court appointment, and record the ordinary details a caregiver would need.

paragraphs: Choose a willing person to raise your children, identify a backup, and have the nomination documented correctly for your jurisdiction. Also arrange who would help immediately if neither parent could be reached. A nomination is not an automatic custody transfer, and a practical care note does not replace the legal process.

The difficult question is often not who loves the children most. It is who could realistically provide daily care, maintain important relationships and take on the responsibility over years. This US planning checklist helps prepare that decision and the conversation with a lawyer. It cannot determine custody, override another parent's rights or guarantee a court's choice.

body.heading: Work through the guardian decision
items: Consider the child's existing relationships, stability, cultural and language connections, support needs and the effect of moving.
Assess the proposed caregiver's willingness and practical capacity, not just their finances or family position. Ask how the change affects their household.
Discuss siblings explicitly: whether they could remain together, what space is available and what support would be needed.
Ask the first choice and backup separately, explain the role and allow time for a considered answer. Do not record silence as agreement.
Take the choice and any custody documents to a qualified adviser. Confirm how to nominate someone and how the actual appointment would work.
Prepare an immediate-care plan and a short routine note. Review the arrangement after family, health, residence or relationship changes.

body.heading: Nomination and appointment are different
paragraphs: [California Courts](https://selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/guardianship) provides a clear state example: guardianship of the person involves a court order giving an adult responsibility for a child's care and legal decisions. Its [statutory will form](https://selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2026-02/6240-Statutory-will-form.pdf) includes a parental nomination. These are related steps, not interchangeable ones, and California's form is not a national template.

Do not assume that writing a name means a court will "almost always" approve it. Parental rights, applicable standards, objections, eligibility and the child's situation matter. A surviving parent's role must be addressed under the applicable law, not treated as displaced by another parent's preference in a binder.

body.heading: Three jobs that need separate answers
rows: Who can reach and care for the children tonight?
Agreed contact, pickup arrangements and locally appropriate authority.
Who would you nominate if a guardian is needed?
Proper legal nomination and location of the document.
Who would manage funds for the child and on what terms?
Relevant estate-plan documents and professional contact.

body.heading: Example: two people doing different jobs
paragraphs: Invented example: two parents prefer a sister who lives several hours away as their long-term nominee. A nearby friend agrees to collect the children in an emergency through the school's approved pickup process. A backup nominee is asked too. The parents discuss legal documentation with an attorney instead of assuming the pickup permission appoints a guardian.

The sister would not necessarily manage inherited funds. That question is considered separately, with advice about the appropriate arrangement. The care page records school contacts, allergies and current care-plan locations, while financial and legal documents remain securely held. It does not contain improvised medical instructions or a promise that the sister will receive custody automatically.

body.heading: Ask about daily life, not an idealized role
paragraphs: Discuss where the children would live, school changes, existing support, sibling relationships and contact with important adults. Ask what resources would make the arrangement feasible. A person can be loving and still unable to take several children, manage specialist needs or relocate.

Avoid turning age, income or marital status into a single deciding score. The practical question is capacity for this child in this family. Where appropriate, seek professional guidance on considering the child's views without making them feel responsible for an adult legal decision.

body.heading: Give the person room to answer

items.line: If a guardian were needed for the children, would you consider being our first choice? We want to discuss what it would involve, including school, housing and support. Please take time; an honest no is useful information.
Would you consider serving as the backup if our first choice could not? We would like you to know the practical plan and the document location, not just appear as a name on a page.

body.heading: Cover a short absence separately
paragraphs: A work trip, hospital admission or temporary inability to collect a child may call for a different authorization than full guardianship. Ask the school, clinician and a qualified local adviser what permissions are required for the actual task. Do not assume school pickup authority includes medical consent or custody.

Keep an emergency contact list where the appropriate people can use it. Make sure the first responder to the practical problem knows who is expected to help next. If there is no safe adult available now, use appropriate emergency or child-welfare support rather than waiting to finish an estate-planning checklist.

body.heading: When legal advice should come first
paragraphs: Get specific advice for co-parent disagreement, existing custody orders, family violence, interstate or international placements, tribal-law issues, significant disability-related needs or disputed parental capacity. Do not use this checklist to persuade a school to ignore a custody order or to remove a child across a jurisdictional boundary.

Where parents disagree, document questions and concerns for counsel rather than assuming competing private nominations will settle the conflict. If someone is pressuring you to sign, pause and seek independent help. A plan intended to protect a child should not be built on hidden disagreement about legal authority.

body.heading: Keep the supporting note practical
paragraphs: A routine note can explain school, transport, important relationships, current health-plan locations, food needs and what helps the child through unfamiliar days. Keep sensitive information limited to those who need it. Date the note and distinguish a settled arrangement from a preference still being discussed.

Review the nominee's willingness after a major change. A conversation from years ago does not establish present capacity. Tell the relevant people where current documents are held and who can explain them. Do not distribute multiple unsigned drafts as if they are operative instructions.

items.q: Does naming a guardian in a will automatically give custody?
items.a: No. A nomination records your choice, but the applicable court and legal process determine appointment when needed. Another parent's rights and the child's circumstances still matter. Ask a qualified adviser how your jurisdiction treats nominations and what additional emergency-care arrangements are appropriate.

items.q: Should the guardian also manage inherited money?
items.a: Not necessarily. Daily caregiving and managing property are different responsibilities. They may be handled by the same person or through separate arrangements, depending on the plan and law. Discuss the options with an estate-planning professional rather than assuming a care nomination also settles every financial question.

items.q: What if nobody can agree to take the children?
items.a: Do not invent a settled choice. Identify trusted adults, discuss realistic support and ask a qualified adviser about available planning options. Make an immediate-care plan where possible and record the unresolved long-term question. If children lack safe care now, address that urgent situation through appropriate local services.
